# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-5 (Extended v68)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; 1809 (Pope's arrest); 1811 (Bishop's synod); 1813 onward (Napoleon's decline); 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, early October—evening/night of Valjean's theft and flight; Battle of Waterloo/Hougomont siege, June 17-18; June 18-19 evening/night post-battle looting); 1817 (carrier sighting; young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion); 1818 spring (Montfermeil cook-shop, Thénardier family, Fantine's arrival); 1819-1821 (Madeleine's mayoral appointment and town transformation); 1823 January (Fantine's arrest and street incident; Javert's revelation; Valjean's acute crisis; TRIAL SEQUENCE: Journey to Arras through February, arriving evening near eight o'clock; TRIAL EVENING SESSION; witnesses testify; Valjean reveals himself; acquittal of Champmathieu; arrest order issued; RETURN TO M. SUR M. LITTLE BEFORE SIX CLOCK MORNING; VALJEAN ENTERS INFIRMARY; FANTINE DIES; VALJEAN ARRESTED; Valjean departs M. sur M. marching toward Paris carrying bundle, dressed in workman's blouse); 1815 June 18-19 (midnight onward: post-Waterloo looting; mysterious prowler in blouse on hollow road of Ohain; sutler's wagon hidden behind hovel at Mont-Saint-Jean to Braine-l'Alleud road angle; woman seated in wagon among coffers and packages); October 1823 (ship Orion enters Toulon port after heavy weather, for repairs); **November 17, 1823 (convict Jean Valjean fell from rigging into sea between Orion and frigate Algésiras, drowned, body not found, presumed entangled in Arsenal piles; newspaper account published)**; **December 24-25, 1823 (Christmas Eve-Christmas Day, Montfermeil tavern scene; mysterious man in yellow coat searches Paris afternoon, eluded police, boarded Lagny coach at half-past four, disembarked Chelles, traveled to Montfermeil forest conducting careful search, encountered Cosette with water bucket, brought her to hostelry; produced doll and offered it; Cosette's overwhelming emotional response; late evening drinkers departed; man remained; after two o'clock morning removed shoes, took candle, searched house, discovered Cosette's wretched sleeping quarters and children's shoes awaiting Christmas gifts; was on point of withdrawing upon this sight; Thénardier read newspaper while wife slept)**; **December 25, 1823 onwards (mysterious man negotiated with Thénardier for Cosette's release; produced three bank-bills; Thénardier initially resisted, demanded proof of parentage; man produced paper from pocket-book showing accounting of Cosette's debts—January 120 francs owed, February 500-franc bill, received 300 francs end February and 300 francs beginning March, nine months at 15 francs/month equals 135 francs, total 35 francs still owing, man gave 1,500 francs; Cosette departed with man, no longer in rags; Thénardier pursued but lost trail near Livry heading toward Gagny forest; Cosette left Thénardier tavern with man; she was leaving that hated and hating house)**; **Spring of second year (1824 onward): New narrative period begins**.

## Primary Locations
M. sur M.; Montfermeil (between Livry and Chelles, southern edge of lofty plateau separating Ourcq from Marne; small village in 1823 with pleasure-houses, church, spring near road to Chelles, ponds toward Gagny, water-carrier earning eight sous daily; toy-shop opposite Thénardier hostelry; Boulanger Lane; turf alley covering arch of ancient aqueduct of Abbey of Chelles; large clearing on right of Avenue de Bellevue); Dunstead (harbor town in England; Dungate nearby); Ravenmere; Staveford; Ostcombe; Kelford; Arras; Nivelles; La Hulpe; Braine-l'Alleud; Lillois; Genappe; Hal; Tongres; Hougomont; Mont-Saint-Jean; Belle-Alliance; Abbey of Villiers forest; Rossomme farm; Ohain; Chapelle-Saint-Lambert; Wavre; Dion-le-Mont; Plancenoit; forest of Paris; Papelotte; Frischemont; Boitsfort; Groenendael; Soignes forest; Waterloo battlefield; Toulon port; Brest; Gagny; Chelles; Livry; Yarlby; England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere, Dunby); Paris (Boulevard de l'Hôpital, faubourg Saint-Marceau, Salpêtrière, Porte Saint-Martin, blind alley of La Planchette, Plat d'Etain coach office); Mediterranean; Balearic Isles; Nanterre; Suresnes; Switzerland; Pyrenees.

## The Mysterious Man in Yellow Coat
**Identity and Appearance**: Man in yellow coat; threadbare frock-coat; battered hat; walked Paris Boulevard de l'Hôpital seeking lodgings; appeared foreign to Paris; observed by M. le Duc de Havré (captain of guard) during king's passage Christmas afternoon two o'clock; drew notice of royal police; one agent ordered to follow; man eluded agent by plunging into deserted streets of faubourg as twilight fell; agent lost trace; report made to M. le Comte d'Anglès, Minister of State, Prefect of Police. **Exceptional strength noted**: grasped Cosette's water bucket with single hand; walked tolerably fast carrying bundle and cudgel; laid both on bench with ease; on point of withdrawing upon sight of Cosette's sleeping pallet and Christmas shoes but was interrupted.

**Movements Christmas Afternoon/Evening**: Passed theatre of Porte Saint-Martin at quarter-past four where _The Two Convicts_ was being played; halted to read poster; entered blind alley of La Planchette; entered _Plat d'Etain_ coach office; boarded coach to Lagny at half-past four, intended destination Chelles only; disappeared like he "dived through the earth"; traveled with great strides through Chelles; followed road to Montfermeil rapidly; walked like person acquainted with country; in forest began careful examination of all trees advancing step by step as if seeking mysterious road known to himself alone; appeared to lose himself, paused in indecision; arrived at clearing with great heap of whitish stones; stepped up briskly, examined stones through mists; went to large tree covered with vegetation warts, passed hand over bark counting warts as if seeking to recognize.

**Encounter with Cosette and Actions at Hostelry**: While walking through thicket espied tiny shadow moving with groan, depositing burden, taking it up; drew near, perceived very young child laden with enormous bucket of water; approached child, silently grasped bucket handle; walked tolerably fast; Cosette followed without difficulty, no longer felt fatigue; raised eyes toward man with tranquillity and indescribable confidence; entered hostelry; laid bundle and cudgel on bench, seated at table; produced doll and offered it to Cosette; tavern-keeper scented acquisitive potential; all other travellers withdrew and stared from distance with respectful awe; remained at table in thoughtful attitude through midnight mass and beyond; after Thénardier retired to corner with candle and newspaper, removed shoes, took one candle, left room searching, discovered Cosette's pallet under staircase, traversed adjoining dark room observing Éponine and Azelma's beds and cradle with sleeping boy, examined fireplace containing two coquettish children's shoes and Cosette's wooden sabot covered with ashes and dried mud—Cosette had placed shoe on hearth with touching childhood trust awaiting Christmas gift.

**Negotiation with Thénardier (December 25)**: Man approached Thénardier on second morning or afterwards; Thénardier initially claimed affection for Cosette, stated he brought her up, said she costs money but he loves her, she is like his own child, he wants to keep her to babble about house. Man responded firmly: "One does not require a passport to travel five leagues from Paris. If I take Cosette away, I shall take her away, and that is the end of the matter. You will not know my name, you will not know my residence, you will not know where she is; and my intention is that she shall never set eyes on you again so long as she lives. I break the thread which binds her foot, and she departs. Does that suit you? Yes or no?" Thénardier persisted, demanding he not give away child to passer-by like that, insisted on knowing what becomes of her, demanded "petty scrap of paper, some trifle in the way of a passport." Man opened pocket-book, drew forth simple little paper, unfolded and presented to Thénardier, stating: "Monsieur Thénardier, in January last, the mother reckoned that she owed you one hundred and twenty francs. In February, you sent her a bill of five hundred francs; you received three hundred francs at the end of February, and three hundred francs at the beginning of March. Since then nine months have elapsed, at fifteen francs a month, the price agreed upon, which makes one hundred and thirty-five francs. You had received one hundred francs too much; that makes thirty-five still owing you. I have just given you fifteen hundred francs." Man folded up three bank-bills, thrust them into his pocket.

**Pursuit and Loss of Trail**: Thénardier ran out in haste but made mistake, turned right first; neighbors put him on right track; the Lark and man seen going toward Livry; Thénardier followed with great strides, talking to himself, pondering bundle of clothes prepared beforehand for child, mysteries concealed, secrets of wealthy as sponges of gold; said "I am an animal." When reached turn of road to Livry, calculated he should see old man and child; looked far as vision reached, saw nothing; made fresh inquiries; informed man and child gone toward forest in direction of Gagny; Thénardier hastened in that direction. Near brushwood of turf alley covering arch of ancient aqueduct of Abbey of Chelles, caught sight of man's hat over top of brushwood; recognized man and Cosette were sitting there; child could not be seen on account of small size but head of her doll was visible. Trail then lost.

**Character Analysis**: Fate of many men to live half submerged; in calm and even situation possessed all required to make honest trader and good bourgeois; yet had all requisites for blackguard under certain circumstances; shopkeeper in whom there was some taint of monster; Satan must have occasionally crouched in corner of hovel and fell a-dreaming in presence of this hideous masterpiece.

## Cosette's Condition and Departure (Winter 1823)
**Physical and Mental State**: Age 8; serving as servant to Thénardiers at Montfermeil; barefooted in winter; wore rags; bare feet thrust in wooden shoes; eye black from blow of Madame Thénardier's fist; weak but did coarse work; thin arms; wet and tiny hands. **Fear now habitual**: Fear diffused all over her; covered with it; drew elbows close to hips; made her occupy minimal space; allowed only absolutely necessary breath; became habit of her body; in depths of eyes astonished nook where terror lurked.

**Labor**: Subjected to double pressure of man and woman; overwhelmed with blows; barefooted in winter; ran upstairs and down, washed, swept, rubbed, dusted, ran, fluttered, panted, moved heavy articles; no mercy.

**Water Crisis and Night Errand (Christmas Eve)**: Woman turned faucet; thin stream trickled; declared "there is no more water!"; sent for water from spring despite darkness and terror; descended Boulanger Lane; encountered woman who called her "the Lark"; chose to flee through village and enter forest at run. **Spring journey**: Seven or eight minutes' walk from village edge to spring; guided by instinct; felt in dark for young oak leaning over spring; found branch, clung, bent down, plunged bucket; while bent over, fifteen-sou piece fell silently into water from apron pocket (neither saw nor heard it fall); drew out bucket nearly full. **Return in darkness**: Stared at great ruddy star near horizon traversing dense mist—unfamiliar, terrified her; planet resembled luminous wound; seized by black enormity of nature; began counting one through ten to escape singular state; terror unconquerable returned; one thought—flee at full speed through forest; yet dared not without bucket; seized handle with both hands; could hardly lift; advanced dozen paces, bucket full and heavy; forced to set down, breathe, resume march; walked bent forward like old woman; weight strained and stiffened thin arms; forced to halt; cold water splashing fell on bare legs; proceeded alone in depths of forest at night in winter—no one but God witnessed. **Lost coin in spring**: Fifteen-sou piece fell from apron pocket while drawing water; neither saw nor heard it; loss unknown to her.

**At Hostelry Christmas**: Following mysterious man back without difficulty; Madame Thénardier sent her to bed; Cosette began rocking swaddled sword singing "My mother is dead! my mother is dead!"; observed no one watched; crept out on hands and knees; seized doll in instant, returned to place under table. **Doll produces overwhelming emotion**: rare happiness contained all violence of voluptuousness; took doll, laid it gently on floor with veneration mingled with despair; without taking eyes from it, clasped hands, wrung them; wept, burst out sobbing—unprecedented for her; when man approached with doll, gazed at him as at sun; slowly retreated, hid herself at extreme end under table; face flooded with tears, eyes began to fill with strange beams of joy; felt moment comparable to being told "Little one, you are the Queen of France." Now sleeps in triangular recess under staircase with straw pallet, tattered coverlet, no sheets; placed wooden sabot on fireplace hearth in Christmas Eve tradition, awaiting gift from good fairy.

**Departure with Man**: As Cosette was no longer in rags, many did not recognize her. Cosette was going away—with whom she did not know; whither she knew not. All that she understood was that she was leaving the Thénardier tavern behind her. No one had thought of bidding her farewell, nor had she thought of taking leave of any one. She was leaving that hated and hating house. **In harbor town of Dunstead**: She hastily set about her regular morning duties. That louis (CHANGE: later revealed as part of 1,500 francs paid) which she had about her, in the very apron pocket whence the fifteen-sou piece had fallen on the night before, distracted her thoughts. She dared not touch it, but she spent five minutes gazing at it with her tongue hanging out. As she swept the staircase, she paused, remained standing there motionless, forgetful of her broom and of the entire universe, occupied in gazing at that star which was blazing at the bottom of her pocket.

## Thénardier Family Dynamics
**Male Thénardier**: Composite rascal of uncertain origin—probably Fleming from Lille in Flanders; exaggerated Waterloo prowess; tattered conscience; belonged to marauding sutlers of June 18, 1815 epoch. Peculiar rectilinear gestures; fine talker; appeared educated with improper pronunciation; cunning, greedy, slothful, clever; rarely wrathful but when enraged, terrible—bore deep furnace of hatred; attentive and penetrating; highly intelligent; had look of sailors; "a statesman"; possessed certain cold tranquil laugh, particularly dangerous. Single thought: enrichment; understood hospitality as merchandise. Articulated aphorisms: duty to sell stews, repose, light, fire, dirty sheets, servant, lice, smile; stop passers-by, empty small purses, honestly lighten heavy ones; make traveller pay for everything. Distinguishes between "going to bed" (twenty sous) and "reposing" (twenty francs). **Christmas night and after**: Remained seated at corner table, lighted candle, read Courrier Français; initially resisted stranger's claim to Cosette, feigned affection, demanded proof; upon receiving accounting paper and 1,500 francs, accepted; pursued man and child toward Livry but lost trail.

**Female Thénardier**: Formidable creature; loved no one except her daughters; feared no one except her husband. Jealous of husband; deemed thin yellow man must be coveted by all. Capable of wrath equal to husband's but his rarer; hideous, hyena mouth; wrath flashing in eyes; inspires terror in Cosette. Expressed disdain for threadbare coat and battered hat. **Christmas evening**: Hated mysterious stranger worse than anyone in world at that moment; necessitated controlling herself; habituated to dissimulation through copying husband; emotions more than she could endure; made haste to send daughters to bed; asked man's permission to send Cosette to bed also, added with maternal air "for she has worked hard all day"; expressed fury at stranger's gift, called doll "forty-franc" and Cosette "jade worth forty sous"; questioned if he would address her as "Your Majesty" like Duchesse de Berry; complained of expenses: license, imposts, door and window tax, hundredths; declared government demands terrible deal of money; lamented having daughters, stated no need to bring up other people's children; claimed price of salt is scandal; asserted they do not ask charity and cannot bestow it; earn nothing and pay out greatly. **At two o'clock morning declared herself vanquished and went to bed** after saying to husband "Do as you like."

**Éponine and Azelma**: Two pretty little girls, more bourgeois than peasant in looks, very charming; one with shining chestnut tresses, other with long black braids hanging down back; both vivacious, neat, plump, rosy, healthy; warmly clad with maternal art; springtime not wholly effaced; light emanated from both; on the throne in toilettes, gayety, noise they made—sovereignty. When entered, Thénardier said to them in grumbling tone full of adoration, "Ah! there you are, you children!" **Playing with cat**: executed important operation—got hold of cat; threw doll on ground; Éponine swathing little cat in spite of mewing and contortions in quantity of clothes and red and blue scraps; while performing this work saying to sister in sweet adorable language of children: "You see, sister, this doll is more amusing than the other. She twists, she cries, she is warm. See, sister, let us play with her. She shall be my little girl. I will be a lady. I will come to see you, and you shall look at her. Gradually, you will perceive her whiskers, and that will surprise you. And then you will see her ears, and then you will see her tail and it will amaze you. And you will say to me, 'Ah! Mon Dieu!' and I will say to you: 'Yes, Madame, it is my little girl. Little girls are made like that just at present.'" **Sent to bed Christmas evening; sleep in small white beds in room adjoining Cosette's pallet; placed coquettish shoes on fireplace hearth Christmas Eve awaiting gifts from good fairy**.

**Little boy**: Cried all evening; lies asleep in uncurtained wicker cradle behind Éponine and Azelma's beds.

## Dunstead/Kelford/Ravenmere Community
- **Pewyn**: counted coins twice, penny short; gave Nylia Corrford solemn promise to rebuild fallen wall at Quenford; asked Nylia "Will it rain, do you think?" on morning with frost silvering hedges; Nylia only shrugged; (CLAIM: Pewyn Stenenridge walked long way round to avoid muddy square)
- **Yewyn Corrford**: appeared tired; bought ribbon, regretted it; **married Tatho Brackick at Ravenmere before spring was out** (1824); complained of aching back as usual; gave Lura Haskick solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Dungate; gave solemn promise to Yera Haskick to carry sealed letter to Dungate
- **Ulrald Corrford**: complained of aching back; gave Lura Haskick solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Stenson family; **whispered that Tatho Brackick had secretly married Fewyn Stenworth, but nobody could say where or when** (RUMOR)
- **Nylia Corrford**: complained of aching back; gave Pewyn solemn promise to rebuild fallen wall at Quenford; read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half saints; laughed at story nobody else found funny; fell asleep in chair before fire caught; hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step; only shrugged at question about rain; stated "The price of salt is a scandal"
- **Yera Haskick**: gave Yewyn Corrford solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Dungate; late one night confided to Kassa Brackick that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood (CLAIM)
- **Lura Haskick**: recipient of Ulrald's debt-payment promise; mended torn sleeve by window, said little; shrugged about rain; asked "Will it rain, do you think?"; **apprenticed anew and became a cooper**
- **Kassa Brackick**: told Yewyn "price of salt is scandal"; received Yera's confidence about mill ledger
- **Elra Corrford**: sorted old letters by candlelight; watched clouds, predicted rain wrongly
- **Marald Corrford**: asked about rain; confirmed looking tired; bought ribbon at stall and then regretted it
- **Tatho Brackick**: rode out of Kelford; **married Yewyn Corrford at Ravenmere before spring was out** (1824); couple lived in Ravenmere; **CLAIM: secretly married Fewyn Stenworth before this marriage, location and date unknown (RUMOR per Ulrald)**
- **Rozek Stenenridge**: burned letter after reading; found work in Staveford, moved there, did not return; mended torn sleeve by window and said little; watched clouds and predicted rain wrongly; won copper chalice from wife at cards fairly, and kept it; CLAIM: Luena followed him to Staveford within the month
- **Luena Stenenridge**: counted coins twice and still came up a penny short; **CLAIM: followed Rozek to Staveford within the month**
- **Nylia Corrford's eldest son**: **kept promise made to Rozek Stenenridge: task (plant an orchard on slope above Yarlby) was done by harvest** (1823)
- **Rovus and Wenelle Lindmere**: wed at Ostcombe with half parish looking on; couple lived in Ostcombe
- **Fenelle**: laughed at story nobody else found funny
- **Isric Thornmere**: asked Vesmira if it will rain; Vesmira only shrugged
- **Jotho and Gadrek** (Ostcombe): agreed price of salt is scandal
- **Thizek Stenenridge**: walked long way round to avoid muddy square

## Main Characters Status
- **Jean Valjean**: Dead (drowned November 17, 1823, at Toulon)
- **Fantine**: Dead (buried in pauper's grave, January 1823)
- **Cosette**: Age 8; liberated from Thénardier servitude; departed with mysterious man; now in harbor town of Dunstead; no longer in rags; carries louis distracted her thoughts
- **Mysterious Man**: Successfully negotiated Cosette's release from Thénardier with accounting paper and 1,500 francs; traveled with Cosette toward Dunstead; man's true identity and origins remain unknown
- **Napoleon Bonaparte**: Defeated, imprisoned at Saint Helena

## Themes and Narrative Development
- Redemption through mysterious intervention; stranger as instrument of Providence liberating child from servitude
- Cosette's transformation: from fear-habituated servant to child carried toward new life; doll as bridge between despair and hope
- Thénardier's moral duality: capable of appearing honest tradesman yet containing taint of monster; greed ultimately overcome by payment of substantial debt
- Accounting and moral economy: mysterious man's careful reckoning of Cosette's worth and Thénardier's true debts; settlement through numbers and law rather than sentiment
- Mundane provincial life indifferent to individual dramas; salt prices, promised labors, approaching rain, church bells; world continues; Dunstead harbor life as counterpoint to forest drama
- Transition from winter darkness to approaching spring; narrative moves into second year
